title: Polynomial-factor approximation of cyclotomic ideal SVP
formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that finds a polynomial-factor approximate shortest nonzero vector in every ideal of every power-of-two cyclotomic ring?

More precisely, do there exist one probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,C,d\) such that, for every \(n=2^k\) with integer \(k\ge1\), and every nonsingular matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) whose column lattice \(I_B=B\mathbb Z^n\) is an ideal of \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\), the following holds? On the explicit binary input \((n,B)\) of length \(L\), every run of \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and
\[\Pr\!\left[A(n,B)\text{ outputs }v\in I_B\setminus\{0\}\text{ with }\|v\|_2\le n^c\lambda_1(I_B)\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad
\lambda_1(I_B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.\]
The constants and program are chosen before the dimension and ideal. The approximation factor depends on dimension, not on coefficient bit lengths. The output must be the full integer coefficient vector \(v\).
why: The central issue is whether the algebraic structure used to make lattice cryptography compact also makes a core worst-case search problem efficiently solvable at polynomial approximation. The selected family is a standard cyclotomic family with growing dimension, not a collection of hand-picked easy ideals. Resolving the question would clarify the computational strength of these structured hardness assumptions. An efficient ideal-SVP algorithm would not, merely by reversing a known security reduction, constitute an attack on every ring-LWE or ring-SIS distribution.
status_note: Reviewed on 16 September 2026. The original 2016 source poses a broad direction; the concrete classical polynomial-time polynomial-factor cyclotomic search target is an explicit editorial specialization. Checked later work gives conditional quantum algorithms at larger approximation factors and algorithms or length results for restricted ideal classes. The September Martin and Wan preprints state hardness in different ring families and/or exact regimes, and their proofs were not independently certified here. No matching resolution of this full selected target was found in the bounded search; source_open records that qualified assessment, not exhaustive certification of openness.

progress.text: The revised Peikert survey asks the broad ideal-lattice advantage question and distinguishes search SVP from easier ideal-lattice gap decisions.
Cramer–Ducas–Wesolowski’s journal article gives a conditional quantum algorithm at an exponential-in-square-root approximation scale, retaining its number-theoretic hypotheses.
Pan–Xu–Wadleigh–Cheng give exact classical algorithms on specified prime and product classes in power-of-two cyclotomic rings.
The revised CRYPTO 2022 paper describes additional easy ideal classes and a restricted knapsack application; its abstract is the checked source here.
The Cui–Li–Zhuang revision treats further rational-prime congruence classes, not every ideal in the family.
Martin claims general-to-ideal reductions in varying totally real number rings, explicitly without control of a selected cyclotomic field.
Wan claims exact cyclic-lattice hardness in a different quotient ring and explicitly separates it from approximation and cryptographic distributions.

importance.reason: A core structured-lattice algorithmic barrier underlying widely used families of cryptographic assumptions. The all-ideals, polynomial-approximation target is substantially broader than a prime splitting subclass or a practical speedup, while the explicit classical specialization is narrower than the entire ideal-lattice research program.

sentences: An ideal in a power-of-two cyclotomic ring is a full integer lattice closed under multiplication by the ring.
The selected question asks for a classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm returning an actual nonzero vector within a fixed polynomial factor of the shortest length.
One program and fixed exponents must work for every dimension and every explicitly supplied ideal basis, with all preprocessing and output charged.
This is an expressly labeled specialization of Peikert’s broad question about algorithmic advantages of ideal-lattice structure.
Conditional quantum algorithms, easy prime-ideal classes and the new exact-hardness claims in other rings do not determine this all-ideals target.

definitions:
Identify \(R_n\) with the integer polynomials of degree less than \(n\), with addition and multiplication reduced modulo \(X^n+1\). Coordinates are ordered as the coefficients of \(1,X,\ldots,X^{n-1}\). The coefficient Euclidean norm is \(\|a\|_2=(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j^2)^{1/2}\). For these dimensions, \(X^n+1\) is the cyclotomic polynomial of conductor \(2n\), so \(R_n\) is the full ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2n})\). The dimension varies without an upper bound.

An integral ideal is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by every ring element. In the supplied coordinates, the input promise is exactly that \(B\) is nonsingular over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(S(B\mathbb Z^n)\subseteq B\mathbb Z^n\), where
\[S(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})=(-a_{n-1},a_0,\ldots,a_{n-2}).\]
Closure under \(S\) and under integer linear combinations gives closure under every ring element. Equivalently, all entries of \(B^{-1}SB\) are integers. Every nonzero integral ideal has a full additive basis of this form. The basis need not be reduced, canonical, circulant or generated by one ring element. Arbitrary prime and composite ideals are included, and no factorization, short generator or special distribution of ideals is promised. Nonsingularity makes \(I_B\) a discrete full-rank lattice, so its positive shortest length is attained.

The input is a dense, explicitly written integer matrix. To fix a binary convention, encode a nonnegative integer \(a\) by \(U(a)=1^\ell 0b\), where \(b\) is the usual binary expansion of \(a\), without leading zeros, and \(\ell\) is its length; use \(b=0\) for zero. Encode a signed integer by a sign bit followed by \(U(|a|)\), with sign zero for zero. Write \(U(n)\) followed by the signed entries of \(B\) in row-major order. Their total length is \(L\). No omitted zeros, succinct matrix circuits or unit-cost large integers are available. Valid outputs list the \(n\) signed coordinates in the same integer encoding; writing every output bit is charged.

The machine has a fixed finite program, alphabet and number of tapes. Each transition reads and writes finitely many tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; an independent fair random bit can be drawn at a charged transition. Time includes reading, arithmetic, any preparation depending on \(n\), and writing the output. The time bound holds on all input strings of length \(L\) and all coin sequences. Mathematical success is required only on promised inputs. Outside the promise, any output is permitted. On a promised input, a failure marker, malformed vector or vector violating the displayed conditions counts as failure. Success probability is over the independent coins for each fixed input, not over a distribution of bases.

No quantum computation, oracle, nonuniform advice, precomputed table depending on the field, unit-group basis or ideal factorization is supplied for free. Such information may be computed only within the stated classical time bound. Polynomial exponents may be large but must be universal. Allowing a fixed multiplicative constant in the approximation would be equivalent after increasing \(c\), since \(n\ge2\).

The norm is fixed explicitly to avoid an embedding ambiguity. For \(\zeta_{2n}=\exp(\pi i/n)\), the canonical embedding lists the \(n\) values \(a(\zeta_{2n}^{2j+1})\), \(0\le j<n\). Its squared Euclidean norm is \(n\sum_j a_j^2\). Thus, in this selected family, canonical and coefficient norms differ by the common factor \(\sqrt n\), which cancels in the relative approximation guarantee. This statement does not identify the two norms in arbitrary number rings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its full negation. A positive answer must specify one finite classical program and universal constants, with a proved bound on every execution and at least \(2/3\) success on each promised basis. A negative answer must rule out every program and every choice of polynomial approximation and time bounds in this model. In particular, for each machine with a global polynomial clock and each fixed exponent \(c\), some promised input must have success probability below \(2/3\). A conditional consequence under an unproved complexity assumption is not an unconditional negative answer. Algorithms for selected ideals, quantum algorithms, superpolynomial approximation factors, or uncharged field preprocessing do not establish this target. Producing or estimating only the shortest length does not satisfy the required search output.

source_formulation.text: Peikert's 2016 Question 3 asks broadly whether ideal-lattice algorithms, possibly quantum, can substantially outperform general-lattice algorithms, and whether such advances extend to ring-SIS/LWE. It does not choose a field family, approximation scale or running time. Following the user's instruction to replace broad directions by concrete variants, this card selects the standard search-SVP problem with polynomial approximation and classical randomized polynomial time on power-of-two cyclotomic ideals. This is a documented editorial specialization, not a quotation or equivalent restatement of all of Question 3. It does not ask for a proved separation from every general-lattice algorithm or for a direct cryptographic attack. Existing conditional quantum speedups at larger approximation factors answer other parts of the historical direction without deciding this target.

context_blocks.text: The 2016 survey frames the question as a tradeoff between the efficiency gained from ring structure and possible additional algorithmic weaknesses. Its search problem asks for an actual short vector. This distinction is essential: the same survey explains that certain polynomial-gap decision versions on ideals can be easy even when finding an adequately short vector is not known to be efficient.

Multiplication by \(X\) gives a signed rotation of every coefficient vector in the selected ideal. For example, \(q\mathbb Z^n\) is an allowed ideal with shortest length \(|q|\) for each nonzero integer \(q\). Such easy instances do not determine the worst-case question, which also includes ideals without a short generator supplied in the input. A change of additive basis describes the same ideal; the guarantee must hold for every explicit basis and charges its actual bit length.

General lattice algorithms already give polynomial-time approximations whose factors are much larger than polynomials in dimension. Peikert's §2.2.2 records that historical time–approximation landscape. Restricting to ideal lattices is useful here only if the output quality and full running time meet both polynomial requirements. The earlier broad phrasing “outperform general lattices” is replaced by this testable threshold, without claiming a lower bound for all generic algorithms.

Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski give a quantum algorithm with approximation factor \(\exp(\widetilde O(\sqrt m))\) for cyclotomic conductor \(m\). Their Theorem 5.1 assumes GRH and a class-group generation hypothesis, and its running time also depends polynomially on the real-subfield class number. Polynomial boundedness of that class number is an additional hypothesis used for the advertised polynomial-time consequence. This important advance has a different computation model and a superpolynomial approximation guarantee.

Pan, Xu, Wadleigh and Cheng prove classical polynomial-time exact SVP for prime ideals above rational primes \(p\equiv3,5\pmod8\) in the power-of-two family, and for a specified class of products of such primes. Their introduction stresses that the proportion of easy instances depends on how ideals are sampled. The result does not cover every ideal, and the paper explicitly distinguishes these algorithms from a break of ring-LWE.

The CRYPTO 2022 work of Boudgoust, Gachon and Pellet-Mary extends the easy-instance analysis using ideals preserved by many field automorphisms. Its cryptographic application concerns particular partial Vandermonde knapsack instances. The publisher/ePrint abstract was checked for this scope; it is not evidence of a general polynomial-time algorithm for every ideal.

Cui, Li and Zhuang's January 2026 revision studies further prime-ideal classes. In particular, its Theorem 2 describes shortest lengths above primes \(p\equiv7,9\pmod{16}\). Its hypotheses still restrict the ideals, and a formula for a shortest length is distinct from the full uniform search guarantee. No claim that this preprint resolves the all-ideals target is made here.

Martin’s September 2026 preprint claims a dimension-preserving reduction from generic lattices to ideals in varying totally real monogenic number rings. Theorem 1.1 does not force a chosen cyclotomic field; the surrounding discussion explicitly preserves the possible advantage of field-specific methods. Its separate full-ring-of-integers extension has additional conjectural qualifications. This new hardness claim is not a hardness theorem for the fixed cyclotomic family selected here.

Wan’s September 2026 preprint claims exact Euclidean SVP hardness for ideals of \(\mathbb Z[X]/(X^N-1)\), with \(N=q-1\) for varying odd primes \(q\). That quotient has a different rational algebra from \(\mathbb Q[X]/(X^n+1)\). The paper explicitly makes neither a fixed-factor approximation claim nor a cryptographic key-distribution claim. Even if its proof is correct, the stated exact cyclic result does not determine this polynomial-factor cyclotomic search question.

A worst-case-to-average-case security reduction has a direction: an algorithm for the average-case cryptographic problem would solve an associated worst-case lattice problem with stated parameters. An algorithm for the worst-case lattice problem does not automatically run that implication backwards. The historical second question about direct ring-SIS/LWE attacks therefore remains separate from this card’s selected algorithmic target.
